Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves, many Americans exhibit short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for not assimilating. They have convinced themselves that, instead of adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They go ballistic over little things -- Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English." Yet, even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly upon their immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy or Poland, he jumped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, ripped out his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even while Americans complain about how the current crop of immigrants aren't like their predecessors, they miss the irony: At the time, there were people who said the same thing about their ancestors; the Germans were thought to not be like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish etc. And the Chinese weren't like anyone who had come before them, and so they were labeled "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California, which is home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would do a feature. And, in the days that followed, someone would write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people weren't melting into the pot. Yet, there is more melting going on than one might think, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three kinds of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, etc.); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, etc.); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, etc.). Far from discovering that recent immigrants are ducking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival." Of course, individual groups still fall behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. But, overall, the news is good. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, they wouldn't stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether the immigrants are ready or not. Those are the facts. Of course, fear doesn't listen to facts. That is something else that hasn't changed. Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) — Many Americans who question whether today’s newcomers integrate as rapidly as earlier immigrant generations tend to be impatient—and historically forgetful. Ruben Navarrette Jr. points out that accusations of failing to assimilate have followed immigrants throughout U.S. history.

Critics often assume that modern immigrants, most of whom arrive from Latin America or Asia, have no interest in adjusting to American traditions and instead want the country to change for them. Even minor cultural signs can provoke outrage, including Mexican flags, mobile taco vendors, bilingual children’s programs at libraries, and automated phone systems that say “press one for English.”

At the same time, many of these critics romanticize their own immigrant forebears. In this mythical version of the past, a grandfather from Poland, Italy, Germany, or Ireland stepped off the ship, wrapped himself in the U.S. flag, instantly gave up his original language and culture, and sang “Yankee Doodle Dandy.” That story ignores reality. German immigrants did, in fact, establish communities in Milwaukee and produce beer and cheese. Irish newcomers settled in Boston and joined groups such as the Hibernian Society to maintain their cultural identity and traditions.

There is also considerable irony in complaints that present-day immigrants differ from those who came earlier. Every previous wave faced similar criticism. Germans were said to be unlike the English; the Irish were contrasted with the Germans; Italians were viewed as different from the Irish; and so on. Chinese immigrants were considered unlike every group before them and were branded “unassimilable” by that period’s equivalents of Tom Tancredo. In that respect, little has changed.

Growing up in Central California, an area with a substantial Southeast Asian immigrant community, I saw thousands of people attend Hmong New Year celebrations. The local newspaper would publish a feature about the event, and soon afterward an angry reader would send a letter to the editor arguing that the participants were refusing to join America’s cultural “melting pot.”

A new Manhattan Institute report, however, suggests that considerably more integration is taking place than many people realize. Presented as the first yearly *Index of Immigrant Assimilation*, the study was authored by Duke University professor Jacob Vigdor. It examined assimilation in three areas. Economic integration included factors such as education, employment, and homeownership. Cultural integration covered measures including English-language ability, intermarriage, and family size. Civic integration considered citizenship, military service, political involvement, and related indicators.

Rather than finding that recent arrivals are avoiding assimilation, the report concluded that immigrants who arrived during the last 25 years have integrated faster than comparable immigrants did a century earlier—even though modern newcomers differ more from native-born Americans when they first enter the country.

Certain immigrant populations still lag in particular areas. Chinese and Indian immigrants register low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants score relatively low in economic integration. Canadian and Indian immigrants show lower civic assimilation because relatively few become U.S. citizens.

The broad picture, nevertheless, is encouraging. More than two centuries after its founding, the United States remains highly effective at absorbing immigrants into society. Even groups that might attempt to resist integration would have little chance of stopping it. Assimilation occurs regardless of whether newcomers are prepared for it.

Those are the facts, but fear is rarely persuaded by evidence—and that, too, remains unchanged.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. serves on the *San Diego Union-Tribune* editorial board and writes a nationally syndicated column, which can be read here. The views presented in this commentary belong exclusively to the author.

Many Americans criticize recent immigrants from Asia and Latin America for supposedly failing to assimilate into mainstream society. They are often accused of expecting American institutions and communities to accommodate their cultures rather than adapting to established norms. Such complaints frequently focus on visible signs of cultural difference, including the display of foreign flags, the popularity of ethnic foods, the availability of bilingual services, and the option to conduct everyday activities in languages other than English.

These criticisms are often accompanied by a romanticized account of earlier immigration. Americans may imagine that their own immigrant ancestors immediately abandoned their native languages, customs, and identities upon arriving in the United States. Historical experience, however, tells a more complicated story. German, Irish, Italian, Chinese, and other immigrant communities maintained their languages, religious practices, foods, celebrations, newspapers, and social organizations—sometimes for generations. Like immigrants today, they were frequently accused of being unwilling or unable to assimilate and were treated as threats to national unity.

The recurring criticism of immigrant cultural celebrations illustrates how persistent these attitudes remain. Objections to events such as Hmong New Year celebrations in California echo earlier hostility toward the public traditions of previous immigrant groups. Although the communities being targeted have changed over time, the underlying suspicion of cultural difference has remained remarkably consistent. What is often described as a new problem of assimilation is therefore better understood as part of a long-standing cycle in American history: newcomers preserve elements of their heritage, face criticism for doing so, and gradually become accepted as part of the nation’s cultural fabric.
outputs.L4:
Critics of immigration often argue that recent arrivals from Asia and Latin America are unwilling—or even unable—to assimilate into American society. They point to immigrants who continue speaking their native languages, maintain traditional customs, live in ethnic neighborhoods, and establish their own businesses, newspapers, churches, schools, and civic organizations. To these critics, such practices suggest a refusal to become fully American.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. challenges this argument by placing contemporary immigration in historical context. Earlier immigrant groups behaved in much the same way. European newcomers formed close-knit communities where they could speak familiar languages, practice their religions, celebrate traditional holidays, and rely on institutions created by people from the same homeland. Chinese immigrants likewise built communities that preserved cultural traditions and provided social and economic support in the face of exclusion and discrimination. These institutions did not necessarily represent a rejection of the United States; they often helped immigrants survive, adapt, and gradually participate in American life.

Yet each major wave of newcomers was met with suspicion. Groups now widely regarded as thoroughly American were once accused of divided loyalties, cultural inferiority, and an inability to fit into the nation. Their languages, religions, food, and social practices were treated as threats to national unity. Over time, however, their children and grandchildren learned English, entered mainstream institutions, and combined elements of their ancestral cultures with a broader American identity.

Navarrette argues that the same process is occurring among Asian and Latin American immigrants today. Retaining a native language or cultural tradition does not prevent immigrants from learning English, working, participating in civic life, or identifying with the United States. Assimilation is rarely immediate, and it does not require the complete abandonment of one’s heritage. It is usually a gradual process that unfolds across generations.

The recurring claim that the newest immigrants are uniquely “unassimilable” therefore says less about immigrants than it does about the country’s short historical memory. Americans often forget that previous generations faced nearly identical accusations. Once a group becomes established, its earlier struggles are minimized, while anxiety shifts toward the next wave of arrivals.

From this perspective, the current backlash against Asian and Latin American immigrants is not evidence of a new assimilation crisis. It is another version of an old pattern: newcomers preserve parts of their culture, established citizens interpret that preservation as resistance, and time eventually shows that cultural continuity and American belonging can coexist. Navarrette’s comparison suggests that contemporary immigrants are not failing to assimilate. Rather, they are following a path traveled by many immigrant communities before them.
